title: The Lotus Sutra (Fall Class Part 1)
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the fall class on the Lotus Sutra by asking students to notice how they do zazen, then offers three ways to read the text: historical, devotional, and practical. Nomon tells of reading the Diamond Sutra in a Zurich hotel the night before meetings with Swiss bankers, and sketches the sutra's history and the paths of Shravaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva. Students then read chapter 2 on skillful means in Gene Reeves's translation, where the Buddha twice refuses Shariputra's request to teach and five thousand listeners walk out. The homework is to look for one's own limited views and for the skillful means the universe is offering, and to read chapters 15 and 16.

This is one of the first Mahayana sutras.
We don't know exactly the chronology of when things were written.
We believe it was initially composed sometime around one hundred and fifty before the common era.
And like most of these texts, it grew over the centuries.
It's not like writing a book, where somebody sat down and wrote the Lotus Sutra one day.
Now we have a version of that.
It was an initial set of teachings that correspond to chapters two through nine, and it was all written in verse.
Again, it was written probably in Sanskrit or a variant on Sanskrit.

The way the text is designed, it looks like it's the other way around: they explain it in prose, and then there's a little bridge sentence that says so-and-so now expressed it again in verse.

One school that emerged in Japan about the same time as Dogen, the Nichiren School, has as its main practice chanting the title, because the title suggests the whole meaning of the whole sutra in their hearts.

This is one school that made it to the West, and Tina Turner was a great proponent of this way of practicing.

Some of you may have encountered members of this school who make lots of great claims about all the great things that will happen if you do this practice of chanting the title of the Lotus Sutra in Sino-Japanese.

It's this fabulously self-referential thing.

Like the deep thing to just sit down with your little ink pen and make a copy of the Heart Sutra.

We think now of the Pali Canon as an early representation of that.

The Lotus Sutra and Mahayana in general ended up deciding that there are three huge major ways of understanding, three paths: the path of the Shravaka, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Bodhisattva.
Then the Lotus Sutra is going to talk about one overall way that encompasses all of those.
But there are these three paths.
The Shravakas are basically the early, early Buddhists, and the path of the Shravaka lives on in cultures that maintain early Buddhist practices and teachings.
Thich Nhat Hanh, in talking about this term, says you can think of this as people who practice with others, but their focus is on their own benefit.
These are very simplistic, right?

So that's the Shravakas, the early Buddhist way of being.
The goal is nirvana, which is complete extinction and stillness and freedom.
So the goal is freedom.

Then there's a middle path, which is a little more mysterious, called the Pratyekabuddha path, the path of self-awakening.
It's not really clear this was ever an actual historical movement or a part of Buddhism, though it gets referred to a lot in Mahayana texts.

Scholars think it might have been a way for the Buddhists to put spiritual seekers with other backgrounds into a category: self-awakened people, enlightened people who maybe didn't go through all the usual Buddhist stuff.
[unclear: "Tinahan"] here says that the Pratyekabuddhas are people who have deep insight into their own practice, but they just keep to themselves.

Shravakas practice together, but they aren't as focused on benefiting others.

One thing about the Lotus Sutra that is interesting and sometimes vexing, depending on which of those hats you have on, is that a scholar I like a lot, Donald Lopez, says one of the most intense qualities of the Lotus Sutra is how obsessed with itself it is.
The Lotus Sutra is always talking about the Lotus Sutra, and how much merit you get from studying the Lotus Sutra and reading the Lotus Sutra.
And wonderfully, this Buddha taught the Lotus Sutra, but it's sometimes hard to figure out: well, what is the Lotus Sutra?
If it's talking about itself, what is it?
The title is interesting.
The Sanskrit title is Sadharma Pundarika Sutra.
Sadharma is a special superlative term.
It's not just the Dharma, but the Sadharma, the true doctrine, Sadharma.
And Pundarika is not the usual word for lotus, that's Padma.
Padmasambhava, for example, and Lotus Pose is Padma.
Pundarika is a white lotus, and white lotuses are supremely rare, I guess, and extra special.

It's just the best in every way.
Oh, here's Donald Lopez himself, a quote from him.

*Generations of readers have complained about the Lotus Sutra's incessant praise of itself, so much so that it raises the question of whether the Lotus Sutra is so famous because it promotes itself so well,* that it's a great work because it keeps saying it is, and we all got convinced over the ages.
